meta: In school, the lesson on electric circuits was just pictures in a book; there was no lab, and you were scared of short circuits. Now there are virtual labs: drag batteries and wires on screen and see what happens.

muc.title: Only looking at pictures
muc.text: In school, for the lesson on electric circuits, you only got to look at drawings in the book. You wanted to build one yourself, but there was no lab, and you were scared of short circuits.

muc.title: A virtual lab
muc.text: Now there are virtual labs. You drag batteries, wires and bulbs onto the screen, press run, and see right away whether the bulb lights up.

muc.title: A free library of simulations
muc.text: A well-known one is PhET from the University of Colorado in the US: over a hundred simulations in physics, chemistry, biology and math, free, in many languages.

muc.title: Things you can't do in real life
muc.text: The best part is you can change things you can't change in real life: turn off gravity, zoom into molecules, make time run a hundred times faster.

muc.title: Guess, then press
muc.text: But don't just click for fun. The trick is to guess the result before you run it. When you guess wrong is when you learn the most.

muc.title: Stuck? Ask
muc.text: If you get stuck, take a screenshot and send it to AI, and ask why the result was different from what you guessed.

muc.title: The pendulum
muc.text: Go to the PhET site and choose a simulation, for example the pendulum. Guess whether a longer string makes it swing faster or slower, then press run to check.

muc.title: Role-play with AI
muc.text: For experiments with objects, there are virtual labs. What about practicing conversations with people? Part three: role-play with AI.
